title: The RBI Held Rates and Fired a \$50 Billion Dollar Bazooka Instead. The Rupee Fell Anyway.
excerpt: The central bank bet on NRI deposits and foreign borrowing incentives to shore up the currency. Then oil hit \$97 and wiped out the rally in a single session.
body:
The Reserve Bank of India chose not to raise interest rates last week. It did something more ambitious instead.

In a policy meeting that wrong-footed most analysts, Governor Sanjay Malhotra kept the repo rate at 5.25 per cent and rolled out what traders are calling the most aggressive capital inflows package since the taper tantrum of 2013. The RBI will bear the full hedging cost for banks raising three- to five-year deposits from non-resident Indians under the FCNR(B) route. It will extend the same hedging facility to state-run companies raising external commercial borrowings. And it has widened the Fully Accessible Route, giving foreign investors broader entry into government securities.

The message was clear: if the war economy will not let India cut rates, India will pay to attract dollars from every other direction.

https://x.com/RBI/status/2062771409089438038

Friday's Rally, Monday's Reckoning

Markets loved it — at first. The rupee closed at 94.9450 per dollar on Friday, its biggest single-day gain in two months and its third consecutive weekly advance. Bond yields eased. Traders unwound long dollar positions. State Bank of India estimated the FCNR(B) window alone could pull in more than \$34 billion. ICICI Bank Global Markets went further, projecting the full package could attract \$50 billion.

"We believe the RBI wanted to focus on the FX package this time around — it did not hike rates because it did not want markets to get the impression that it wants to use rate defence for shoring up the rupee," economists at HSBC said in a note.

Then Monday arrived.

Israel struck the Mahshahr petrochemical complex in Iran's southwest — the first hit on an energy site since the April ceasefire — and Brent crude surged past \$97 a barrel. The rupee reversed nearly all of Friday's gains, falling 0.8 per cent to settle at 95.7075 per dollar, its sharpest drop in four weeks.

"The RBI has provided meaningful support to the rupee, but external factors will remain crucial," said Amit Pabari, managing director at FX advisory firm CR Forex. "Any escalation in U.S.-Iran tensions, leading to a stronger dollar or higher oil prices, could temporarily push the pair upwards."

Why NRIs Are at the Centre of This Strategy

The FCNR(B) scheme is not just a central bank manoeuvre — it is a direct appeal to the Indian diaspora.

Non-resident Indians hold an estimated \$140 billion in deposits across Indian banks. When the RBI last deployed this strategy in 2013 during the rupee crisis under then-Governor Raghuram Rajan, NRI deposits surged by \$34 billion in three months and pulled the currency back from the brink.

This time, the stakes are different. The Iran war has kept oil above \$90 for over two months. India imports roughly 85 per cent of its crude. Every \$10 rise in Brent adds an estimated \$15 billion to the annual import bill. Foreign portfolio investors have pulled record sums from Indian markets since the war began in February, and the RBI's foreign exchange reserves have dropped from a peak of \$705 billion to under \$630 billion.

The new FCNR(B) incentive gives NRIs a risk-free premium: the RBI absorbs the hedging cost that would otherwise eat into returns on dollar deposits converted to rupees. For a diaspora already watching their remittances stretch further as the rupee weakens, it is a compelling offer.

The Fed Complication

But the RBI's dollar hunt faces a headwind from Washington. A stronger-than-expected U.S. jobs report for May has revived expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise rates before the end of the year. Higher U.S. yields tend to strengthen the dollar and make emerging-market assets less attractive — exactly the dynamic the RBI is trying to counteract.

Indian equities reinforced the gloom on Monday. The Nifty 50 fell 1.04 per cent to 23,123 and the Sensex shed nearly 1 per cent to 73,524, both closing at two-month lows. Fifteen of sixteen major sectors declined.

The question now is whether the \$50 billion inflow projection holds up if oil stays above \$95 and the Fed signals a hike. The RBI has opened a window. Whether enough dollars actually walk through it depends on a war the central bank cannot control.

Sources: Reuters, ICICI Bank Global Markets, HSBC Research, State Bank of India
